food.text: Until Aden and al-Hudaydah overtook it in the 19th century, Mokha was the principal port for Yemen's capital, Sanaa. The city was so central to the coffee trade from the 16th through the 19th century that it gave coffee its name, "mocha."

In the 19th century, Jeddah was a busy trading hub on the Red Sea, exporting goods such as mother-of-pearl, tortoise shells, frankincense, and spices. Many of these goods then continued onward to Suez, Africa, or Europe.

Even after coffee cultivation spread to other parts of the world, Yemeni Mocha beans, also called Sanani beans after Sana'a, continued to be prized for their distinctive flavor. This reputation grew out of the historic coffee trade centered on the port of Mokha.

Although the port of Mokha gave its name to "mocha" coffee, the beans themselves were never grown there. Instead they were carried from Ethiopia and inland Yemen to Mokha, where they were loaded onto ships for export abroad.

Captain Haines, the colonial administrator of Aden from 1839 to 1854, reported that Mokha had historically imported up to two-thirds of its coffee from Berbera-based merchants. That flow shifted once British-controlled Aden captured the coffee trade away from Mokha in the 19th century.

Within the Ottoman Empire, coffee was prepared in shops called taḥmīskhāne by roasting and crushing the beans in mortars. Coffee houses in Mecca drew a mix of worshippers from the mosques, traders arriving from afar, and travelers passing through the city.
British-controlled Aden captured Mokha's coffee trade during the 19th century. Afterward, England received two-thirds of its coffee this way, avoiding the high duties charged at Mokha.

art.text: Between 1848 and 1860, Turkish forces that had reasserted control of the Hejaz began extensive rebuilding of its sacred sites. Many of the rebuilt sites employed the finest examples of Ottoman design and craftsmanship.
art.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

art.text: Arabic calligraphy was one of the first art forms included in formal education, with the establishment of the Al-Falah schools in Jeddah and Makkah in 1905. It held a highly symbolic position because of its association with transcribing the Quran.

For centuries, Arabic calligraphy and handicrafts were the only forms of visual art commonly practiced in the societies of the Arabian Peninsula. Handicrafts appeared in ornaments, housewares, decoration and clothing, and could commonly be found in local markets.

The initial dismantling of the sites began in 1806, when the Wahhabi army of the First Saudi State occupied Medina. It levelled many structures at the Jannat al-Baqi cemetery, where the Ottoman Turks had erected elaborate mausoleums over the graves. These mausoleums were levelled in their entirety.
art.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

art.text: Calligraphy's firm traditions were passed from generation to generation through the Ijazah system. Sheikh Muhammad Taher Al-Kurdi, a prominent calligrapher who left behind numerous works, is a notable graduate of this system.
In Medina, an attempt was made to demolish the tomb of Muhammad. Widespread vocal criticism from Muslim communities as far away as India eventually led to the abandonment of any attempt on this site.
art.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

art.text: In Mecca, tombs of direct relations of Muhammad were demolished at the Jannatul Mualla cemetery. They included the tomb of his first wife, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid.
art.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

war.text: The First Saudi State, established in 1727 around Riyadh, briefly controlled most of the present-day territory of Saudi Arabia through conquests made between 1806 and 1815. These included Mecca, captured in 1806, and Medina, captured in April 1804.

In 1803 and 1804, the Saudis captured Mecca and Medina and destroyed historical monuments and shrines, including the shrine over the tomb of Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad. They even intended to destroy Muhammad's grave as idolatrous, which caused outrage throughout the Muslim world.
war.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

war.text: Throughout the 19th century, the Al Saud and the Al Rashid fought for control of the interior of what was to become Saudi Arabia. By 1891 the Al Rashid had conclusively defeated the Al Saud and driven them into exile in Kuwait.

In 1801, forces of the First Saudi state stormed the Shia holy city of Karbala, destroying its shrine and monuments and killing more than 5,000 civilians, reflecting Wahhabi rejection of shrine veneration. Abdulaziz bin Muhammad, who led the campaign, was assassinated in 1803 by a young Shia man who had followed him back to Najd.

Political claims made against Turkish control of the Hejaz began the Ottoman–Saudi war of 1811 to 1818. The Saudi defeat forced Wahhabi tribesmen to retreat from the Hejaz into the interior, and Turkish forces then rebuilt sacred sites between 1848 and 1860.
war.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia

war.text: When the Egyptians under the Muhammad Ali dynasty invaded Arabia, they deposed Abdullah bin Saud Al Saud in 1818. They then reoccupied Al-Ahsa and Al-Qatif and reinstated members of Al 'Uray'ir as governors on their behalf.

British campaigns against piracy came in response to the Al Qasimi, who carried out many of the most notable instances of piracy in the Persian Gulf. The British mounted Persian Gulf campaigns in 1809 and 1819, and the latter led to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 with the Sheikhs of the "Pirate Coast".
war.source_title: Arab states of the Persian Gulf

war.text: The Bani Khalid had declined militarily, and tribes such as the Ajman, the Dawasir, the Subay' and Mutayr encroached on their desert territories. An alliance of tribes with Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud defeated them, and battles in 1823 and 1830 brought the rule of the Bani Khalid to a close.

The Battle of Mesaimeer in 1851 raised the Al Thani's influence, when Mohammed bin Thani led local Qatari tribes to defect from Bahrain to the Emirate of Nejd. This began a power struggle with the Al Khalifa, and in 1868 the Qatari–Bahraini War resulted in Qatar's independence from Bahrain, recognized by the British.
war.source_title: Arab states of the Persian Gulf

war.text: Abdulaziz avoided involvement in the Arab Revolt, having acknowledged Ottoman suzerainty in 1914. Instead he continued his struggle with the Al Rashid in northern Arabia, which he finally ended by annexing all of northern Arabia in 1921.

literature.text: The first printing press in Makkah opened in 1883. Printing technology like this later helped texts circulate widely across the Hijaz, as a modern literary movement grew and broader Arab literary movements influenced local writers.

In 1833, Fisher's Drawing Room Scrap Book published an engraving of Samuel Austin's painting of Duba. It was titled Thubare, a Port on the Arabian Coast. A poetical illustration by Letitia Elizabeth Landon accompanied it and recalled the story of the Fairy Pari-Banou and Prince Ahmed.
Rakan bin Hithlain was the most famous sheikh of the Ajman tribe during the 19th-20th century. He was noted for his poetry, and he is still well known in Arabian tribal lore.

Jildiyyah Mountain in Saudi Arabia rises 1,107 meters and appears in Arab poetry. In the 17th-19th century, Orientalists including Doughty, Huber and Anne Blunt described it in their journals, and Julius Ouitinj painted it.

science.text: The Ottoman Empire built the narrow-gauge Hejaz railway between 1900 and 1908, running from Damascus to Medina with a branch line to Haifa. Ordered by Sultan Abdul Hamid II in March 1900, it was the only railway completely built and operated by the Ottoman Empire itself.

The railway's main purpose was to link Istanbul, seat of the Islamic Caliphate, with the Hejaz region and its holy cities, easing the annual hajj pilgrimage toward Mecca. It was also meant to strengthen Ottoman political and economic control over the distant Arabian provinces.

When Sultan Abdul Hamid II came to power, he brought a number of modern marvels to Medina, including a radio communication station, a power plant for the Prophet's Mosque, and a telegraph line linking the city to Constantinople. The Hejaz railway, built between 1904 and 1908, was part of this same wave of modernization.

Ottoman officer Ahmed Reshid Pasha surveyed the Hejaz region during an expedition to Yemen in 1871 to 1873 and concluded that rail was the only feasible way to move Ottoman soldiers through the terrain. His conclusions, along with proposals by other officers such as Osman Nuri Pasha, helped set the stage for the railway project decades later.

Building the railway was costly, with expenses estimated at around 4 million Turkish lira, a sizeable part of the Ottoman budget. The state bank Ziraat Bankasi provided an initial loan of 100,000 lira in 1900, and Sultan Abdul Hamid II called on Muslims worldwide to donate toward construction.

Before the railway existed, hajis, the pilgrims travelling toward Mecca, often never reached their destination along the Hejaz route. Unable to contend with the tough, mountainous conditions, up to 20 percent of them died on the way. The Hejaz railway was a religious symbol as well as a military one, and was conceived in part to spare pilgrims this deadly overland trip.

Within one decade of these modernization projects, the population of Medina multiplied by leaps and bounds and reached 80,000. Around this time the city started falling prey to a new threat, the Hashemite Sharifate of Mecca to the south. Medina went on to endure the longest siege in its history during and after World War I. In the 3-year siege, held by Husayn ibn Ali from 1916, the people faced food shortages, widespread disease and mass emigration.

Under chief engineer Mouktar Bey, the railway finally reached Medina on 1 September 1908, a date chosen because it was the anniversary of the Sultan's accession. To finish in time, builders had to lay some sections of track on temporary embankments across wadis, or dry riverbeds.

politics.text: In 1858, the Ottoman Empire's Tanzimat reforms introduced a new land law that offered legal grounds for displacing the Bedouin from their traditional territory. The law launched an unprecedented land registration process, the Ottoman Tapu, partly meant to boost the empire's tax base.

By 1891 the Al Rashid of Ha'il had conclusively defeated the Al Saud after decades of fighting for control of the interior of Arabia. The Saudis were driven into exile in Kuwait. The rivalry had dominated the rest of the 19th century.

The first Saudi state was destroyed by 1818 by the Ottoman viceroy of Egypt, Mohammed Ali Pasha. A much smaller second Saudi state, located mainly in Nejd, was established in 1824. It was the start of a long struggle with the Al Rashid.

Unlike the expansionist First Saudi state, the Second state was marked by recurring internal divisions, succession disputes and regional rivalries. These weaknesses let the Rashidis of Jabal Shammar surpass the Saudis as the dominant power in central Arabia. After the defeat at Mulayda, Abdul Rahman bin Faisal fled with his family to Ottoman Iraq in 1893 and later Kuwait.

When Egyptian forces under the Muhammad Ali dynasty deposed Abdullah bin Saud Al Saud in 1818, they reoccupied Al-Ahsa and Al-Qatif. They reinstated members of Al 'Uray'ir as governors of the region on their behalf.

In 1902 Ibn Saud seized control of Riyadh, reestablishing the dominance of the Al Saud. He won support from the Ikhwan, a tribal army inspired by Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and led by Sultan ibn Bijad and Faisal Al-Dawish. Established in 1912, the Ikhwan helped him capture al-Hasa from the Ottomans in 1913.

Few Bedouin chose to register their lands under the new Ottoman Tapu system, largely due to illiteracy, unwillingness to pay taxes, and a belief that written land documents had little relevance to their traditional way of life. The Ottomans also did little to enforce the requirement.

The Bani Khalid, once a potent military force in Eastern Arabia, were beset by internal quarrels over leadership as tribes such as the Ajman, Dawasir, Subay' and Mutayr encroached on their territory. Battles in 1823 and 1830 brought their rule to a close. The Ottomans appointed a governor from Bani Khalid over Al-Ahsa once more in 1874, but his rule was also short-lived.

By 1906 Abdulaziz had driven the Al Rashid out of Najd, and the Ottomans recognized him as their client there. In 1913 he took Al-Hasa from the Ottomans, gaining the Persian Gulf coast and what would become Saudi Arabia's vast oil reserves. In 1914 he acknowledged Ottoman suzerainty and avoided the Arab Revolt.

Asir came under Ottoman rule from 1871 until the outbreak of World War I. Its emir, Hasan ibn Ali Al Aid, then "became virtually independent" and attempted to rule from Abha. A struggle ensued between his forces and those of Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi, who eventually set up the short-lived Emirate of Asir under Saudi tutelage.

philosophy.text: European travellers in the 19th century tried to make sense of the Wahhabi movement by comparing it to political movements of their own Age of Revolutions. John Ludwig Burckhardt, author of "Travels in Arabia" (1829), described the Muwahhidun as Arabian locals who resisted Turkish hegemony and its "Napoleonic" tactics.

In the decades after the fall of the First Saudi State, Wahhabi religious thought became more militant. During the civil wars of the 1860s and 1870s, scholars such as Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan (1810-1876) revived Takfiri doctrines, breaking with a moderate approach that had held until 1869.
tags: Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan

philosophy.text: Much of the fierce religious language of this era had a practical purpose. According to the article, most Wahhabi pronouncements of Takfir were motivated by political opportunism, and clerics like 'Abd al-Latif shifted sides multiple times, even after accusing other parties of disbelief and of inciting Fitna.
tags: Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan

philosophy.text: Louis Alexander Corancez's book "Histoire des Wahabis" gave another European reading of the movement, describing it as an Asiatic revolution. Like Burckhardt's works, it shows how outsiders framed Wahhabi ideas through the political categories of their own time.

When the Emirate of Dir'iyyah collapsed in 1818, the Ottomans, through the Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha, leveled the capital Diriyah and slaughtered its inhabitants. They also executed the Al-Saud emir and exiled the emirate's political and religious leadership. A man named Sulayman (1785-1818), a grandson of Ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab, was executed by the Ottomans as well. His Takfiri doctrines, which declared other Muslims to be unbelievers, outlived him and were revived by later scholars.

When the Second Saudi State was established in 1824, its early scholars took a gentler line. Figures like Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan (died 1868) followed a milder approach to Takfir, the practice of declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, until the civil wars of the 1860s and 1870s.
Burckhardt also published "Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys" in 1830, a year after his "Travels in Arabia". The article calls him a Calvinist scholar, and both works were well received in Europe.
tags: Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys

philosophy.text: In the wake of the Ottoman expedition to Hasa, 'Abd al-Latif re-explored the fatwas of past scholars like Ibn Taymiyya on Takfir, Hijra and Al wala wal Bara. He used these doctrines to ensure loyalty and mobilize people against external enemies like the Ottomans and British, and internal ones like the Rafida.
tags: Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan

philosophy.text: Hammad ibn 'Atiq (died 1884), a pupil of 'Abd al-Latif, was the most rigorous and implacable of the anti-Ottoman clerics. He weaponised the doctrine of Al-Wala wal Bara and excommunicated the people of most lands outside Najd, including the Hejaz.
tags: Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan

philosophy.text: After his father's death in 1876, 'Abdullah Aal al-Shaykh became the senior-most scholar in Najd. He kept up the Takfiri polemics of Sulayman and 'Abd al-Latif until his own death in 1920, so this hard-line tradition ran from the 1810s into the 20th century.
tags: Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman Hassan

culture.text: During the second half of the nineteenth century, after the 1850s, steamships began carrying pilgrims to Mecca for the Hajj, adding sea travel to a pilgrimage that had traditionally meant crossing the desert by camel caravan. This gradually changed how believers reached the holy city.

Mecca's role as a pilgrimage hub brought serious health risks: between 1830 and 1930, cholera broke out among the pilgrims gathered there 27 separate times. Repeated epidemics made disease a recurring danger of the Hajj throughout much of the nineteenth century.

In 1853, the British explorer Sir Richard Francis Burton disguised himself as a Muslim in order to complete the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina. His journey became one of the most famous and thoroughly documented pilgrimages of modern times.

In 1909 the German explorer and photographer Hermann Burchardt described the Yemeni port of Mokha as one of the most godforsaken little places in Asia. He wrote that it looked like a city entirely destroyed by earthquakes, the destruction exceeding all his expectations.
